questions.question: What is the difference between Authentication and Authorization in Spring Security?
questions.title: Authentication vs Authorization in Spring Security
questions.direct_answer: Authentication answers 'Who are you?' — it verifies identity by checking credentials and produces an Authentication object stored in the SecurityContext. Authorization answers 'What are you allowed to do?' — it checks the authenticated principal's authorities against the required permissions for a resource. Spring Security enforces these as two distinct, sequential steps.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can clearly articulate the two-step security model and map it to Spring Security's concrete types.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Conflating the two concepts, or not knowing that Authorization can only work after Authentication populates the SecurityContext.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Reference the Authentication interface, GrantedAuthority, AuthenticationManager, and AccessDecisionManager (or the newer AuthorizationManager in Spring Security 6).

sections.title: Authentication Establishes WHO You Are — Authorization Determines WHAT You Can Do
sections.content:
The two concepts are sequential: **authentication must happen before authorization can work.** You cannot decide what a user is allowed to do until you know who they are. Conflating them is the most common mistake in security interviews — and it leads to real bugs like returning 403 to unauthenticated users, which tells attackers the resource exists.

In Spring Security, **authentication** is handled by `AuthenticationManager`, which delegates to one or more `AuthenticationProvider` implementations. The result is an `Authentication` object stored in the `SecurityContextHolder`. This object carries three things: the principal (who), the credentials (proof of identity, usually cleared after success), and a collection of `GrantedAuthority` objects representing roles and permissions.

**Authorization** uses those `GrantedAuthority` values to make access decisions. The `AuthorizationManager` — which replaced the older `AccessDecisionManager` in Spring Security 6 — evaluates whether the authenticated principal holds the required authority for the requested resource. Authorization can happen at two layers: URL-level (in the filter chain via `requestMatchers().hasRole()`) and method-level (`@PreAuthorize` with SpEL). URL-level is faster and coarser. Method-level is finer-grained and can inspect method arguments and return values.

The **401 vs 403 distinction** is the clearest signal of whether you understand this. A 401 means "I don't know who you are — provide credentials." A 403 means "I know who you are, but you're not allowed." Returning 403 for an unauthenticated request leaks information about the resource's existence. Spring Security handles this correctly by default: `AuthenticationEntryPoint` sends 401 for unauthenticated requests and `AccessDeniedHandler` sends 403 for authenticated-but-unauthorized requests.

sections.title: Authentication vs Authorization — Mechanism, Timing, and Spring Components
sections.content:
The distinction maps directly to different Spring Security components with different responsibilities.

| Aspect | Authentication | Authorization |
|---|---|---|
| **Question** | Who are you? | What can you do? |
| **When** | First — before any access decision | After — requires authenticated principal |
| **Failure response** | 401 Unauthorized | 403 Forbidden |
| **Spring component** | `AuthenticationManager` / `AuthenticationProvider` | `AuthorizationManager` / `@PreAuthorize` |
| **Data produced** | `Authentication` object (principal + credentials) | Access decision (allow or deny) |
| **Input** | Credentials (username/password, token, certificate) | `GrantedAuthority` collection + required permission |
| **Storage** | `SecurityContextHolder` (ThreadLocal per request) | Evaluated per request — not stored |
| **Configuration** | `UserDetailsService`, OAuth2, LDAP, SAML | `requestMatchers().hasRole()`, `@PreAuthorize` |

**`GrantedAuthority` is the bridge** between the two phases. Whatever roles you attach during authentication become the vocabulary that authorization rules consume. A `GrantedAuthority` with value `ROLE_ADMIN` attached during login is what makes `hasRole("ADMIN")` return true later. If the roles aren't attached correctly during authentication, every authorization check fails — and the symptom looks like a broken authorization rule when the actual bug is in the authentication phase.

sections.title: URL-Level vs Method-Level Authorization — Choosing the Right Enforcement Point
sections.content:
URL-level authorization (configured in `SecurityFilterChain` with `requestMatchers("/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")`) applies to entire endpoint groups and runs at the filter layer — before any application code executes. This is the fastest line of defense: obviously unauthorized requests are rejected before they consume application resources.

Method-level authorization (`@PreAuthorize`, `@PostAuthorize`) handles fine-grained rules that depend on domain data. "Only the owner can delete their own post" cannot be expressed as a URL pattern — the post ID is in the path, and evaluating ownership requires a repository lookup. `@PreAuthorize("#post.authorId == authentication.principal.id")` performs this check with access to method parameters.

**Use both layers together.** URL rules reject obviously unauthorized requests early. Method-level annotations enforce the ownership and attribute-based checks that URL patterns cannot. The common mistake is relying only on URL-level rules and assuming they're sufficient — a single wildcard misconfiguration can expose an entire section of the API. Defense in depth means `@PreAuthorize` provides a second check even if the URL rule is misconfigured or bypassed.

One practical pattern: configure URL rules broadly (`authenticated()`) and enforce specific role and ownership constraints with method-level annotations. This separates authentication enforcement (URL level) from fine-grained authorization logic (method level), making both easier to audit and test.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Authentication answers 'who are you?'; authorization answers 'what are you allowed to do?'** — authentication must succeed before authorization is evaluated; a 401 means unauthenticated, a 403 means authenticated but unauthorized.
- **`Authentication` object holds the principal and authorities** — after successful authentication, Spring stores an `Authentication` in the `SecurityContext`; `getAuthorities()` returns `GrantedAuthority` objects checked by authorization.
- **`AuthenticationManager` delegates to `AuthenticationProvider` chain** — `DaoAuthenticationProvider` is the default; it loads `UserDetails` from `UserDetailsService` and verifies the password with `PasswordEncoder`.
- **Authorization is evaluated after authentication in the filter chain** — `AuthorizationFilter` (or `FilterSecurityInterceptor`) runs after the authentication filter; checking authorization before authentication completes is not possible.
- **Method security (`@PreAuthorize`) is a second authorization layer** — HTTP security rules protect endpoints; `@PreAuthorize` protects service methods; both can be active simultaneously for defense in depth.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Authentication and authorization are two distinct steps in security. Conflating them is the most common conceptual error in security interviews.

**Authentication — identity verification**
- 'Who are you?' — the user presents credentials (username/password, JWT, certificate)
- Spring's `AuthenticationManager` verifies the credentials
- On success, an `Authentication` object is stored in the `SecurityContextHolder` — containing the principal and their `GrantedAuthority` list
- Failure → `AuthenticationException` → `401 Unauthorized`

**Authorization — permission check**
- 'What are you allowed to do?' — evaluated after authentication succeeds
- Spring checks the `GrantedAuthority` list against the required role/permission for the requested resource
- Failure → `AccessDeniedException` → `403 Forbidden`

**The Spring Security flow**
- Request enters the filter chain
- Authentication filter (e.g., `UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter`) extracts credentials and calls `AuthenticationManager`
- `DaoAuthenticationProvider` loads `UserDetails` via `UserDetailsService`, verifies password with `PasswordEncoder`
- On success, stores `Authentication` in `SecurityContextHolder`
- `AuthorizationFilter` checks `SecurityContextHolder` against the required authorities for the URL

`@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")` on service methods adds a second authorization layer — even if someone bypasses the HTTP-level check, the method-level check still enforces the permission.

questions.question: What are the differences between @PreAuthorize, @Secured, and @RolesAllowed in Spring Security?
questions.title: @PreAuthorize vs @Secured vs @RolesAllowed
questions.direct_answer: @PreAuthorize is the most powerful — it accepts Spring Expression Language (SpEL) and can inspect method arguments, return values, and bean state. @Secured accepts a simple list of role strings and predates SpEL. @RolesAllowed is the JSR-250 standard annotation, also role-string only. For any non-trivial authorization logic, @PreAuthorize is the preferred modern choice.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of method security options and when to use SpEL expressions vs simple role checks.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @Secured or @RolesAllowed and then discovering they cannot express 'only the owner of this resource can edit it' — that requires SpEL in @PreAuthorize.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention @PostAuthorize for filtering return values, @PreFilter/@PostFilter for collections, and that method security requires @EnableMethodSecurity (not @EnableGlobalMethodSecurity in Spring Security 6).

sections.title: @Secured Can't Express 'Only the Owner Can Edit' — @PreAuthorize With SpEL Can
sections.content:
Most developers start with `@Secured("ROLE_ADMIN")` because it looks simple and clean. Then the product requirement arrives: "only the owner can edit their own order." **`@Secured` and `@RolesAllowed` cannot express this.** They accept a list of role strings and perform a simple role membership check — nothing more. Resource-level authorization that depends on the relationship between the authenticated user and the specific data being accessed is impossible with these annotations.

**`@PreAuthorize`** accepts SpEL expressions with access to the method's parameters, the authenticated principal, and Spring-managed beans. `@PreAuthorize("#order.userId == authentication.principal.id")` checks that the order belongs to the current user. `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN') or @orderService.isOwner(#orderId, authentication)")` combines a role check with a service-level ownership check. The `@orderService` bean call is the key capability — you can implement any authorization logic as a Spring bean method and invoke it from the SpEL expression.

The migration from `@EnableGlobalMethodSecurity` (deprecated in Spring Security 6) to `@EnableMethodSecurity` is not optional for new code. The old annotation enabled method security through a voter-based system and required explicit flags (`prePostEnabled=true`). The new annotation enables `@PreAuthorize` by default and uses the cleaner `AuthorizationManager` architecture. Getting this wrong means `@PreAuthorize` silently has no effect — authorization appears to work because no exception is thrown, but all access is permitted. Test your method security annotations.

sections.title: Three Annotations Compared — Capability, SpEL Support, and Enable Configuration
sections.content:
The decision matrix is straightforward once you know what each annotation can express.

| Aspect | @Secured | @RolesAllowed | @PreAuthorize |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Standard** | Spring-specific | JSR-250 (Jakarta EE) | Spring-specific |
| **SpEL expressions** | No | No | Yes — full Spring Expression Language |
| **Role checks** | Yes | Yes | Yes — `hasRole()`, `hasAuthority()` |
| **Parameter access** | No | No | Yes — `#paramName` |
| **Principal access** | No | No | Yes — `authentication.principal.id` |
| **Custom beans** | No | No | Yes — `@beanName.method()` in expression |
| **Post-execution filter** | No | No | Yes — `@PostAuthorize`, `@PostFilter` |
| **Enable with** | `@EnableMethodSecurity(securedEnabled=true)` | `@EnableMethodSecurity(jsr250Enabled=true)` | `@EnableMethodSecurity` (default on) |
| **Spring Security 6 status** | Supported | Supported | Preferred |

**`@PostAuthorize`** evaluates after the method executes and can access the return value via `returnObject`. `@PostAuthorize("returnObject.userId == authentication.principal.id")` ensures a `findById()` call doesn't return another user's data — the method runs, but the result is blocked if the condition fails. **`@PreFilter`** and **`@PostFilter`** apply to collections: `@PreFilter` removes input collection elements that don't satisfy the expression before the method runs; `@PostFilter` removes output elements after.

These post-execution annotations enable **data-level security** without changing every repository method — a powerful pattern for multi-tenant applications where every user should see only their own data.

sections.title: Which Annotation to Use — The Decision Is Simpler Than the Documentation Suggests
sections.content:
**Use `@PreAuthorize` for everything new.** It covers every case that `@Secured` and `@RolesAllowed` cover, plus resource ownership, parameter-based access, and post-execution filtering. The only reason to reach for `@Secured` or `@RolesAllowed` is maintaining consistency in a codebase that already uses them extensively.

For simple role checks, `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")` is slightly more verbose than `@Secured("ROLE_ADMIN")` but provides a consistent pattern throughout the codebase — reviewers don't need to remember which annotation supports which features. `hasRole('ADMIN')` vs `hasAuthority('ROLE_ADMIN')` is worth knowing: `hasRole()` automatically prepends `ROLE_`; `hasAuthority()` checks the exact string. For custom authorities without the `ROLE_` prefix, use `hasAuthority()`.

When SpEL expressions become complex — `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('MANAGER') and @projectService.isTeamMember(#projectId, authentication) and @planLimits.withinQuota(authentication)")` — extract the logic into a custom `PermissionEvaluator` or a dedicated authorization service bean. Complex SpEL expressions are hard to test, hard to audit, and silently do nothing if misconfigured. A testable service method `@PreAuthorize("@authService.canAccess(#projectId, authentication)")` is cleaner and the logic is unit-testable independently.

Enable everything with `@EnableMethodSecurity` on any `@Configuration` class. Add `prePostEnabled=true` is not needed — it's the default. Add `securedEnabled=true` or `jsr250Enabled=true` only if you need those annotation types alongside `@PreAuthorize`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@PreAuthorize` supports SpEL expressions; `@Secured` and `@RolesAllowed` do not** — `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN') or #userId == authentication.name")` uses method parameters in the expression; `@Secured` and `@RolesAllowed` only accept role string literals.
- **`@EnableMethodSecurity` replaces `@EnableGlobalMethodSecurity`** — Spring Security 6.x; `@EnableMethodSecurity(prePostEnabled = true)` enables `@PreAuthorize`/`@PostAuthorize`; the old annotation is deprecated.
- **`@PostAuthorize` evaluates after the method returns** — check if the returned object belongs to the current user: `@PostAuthorize("returnObject.ownerId == authentication.name")`.
- **`@PreFilter` and `@PostFilter` filter collections** — `@PreFilter("filterObject.userId == authentication.name")` removes elements from the input list that the user does not own before the method runs.
- **Method security works through AOP proxies — self-invocation bypasses it** — `this.securedMethod()` inside the same class skips the security proxy; extract to a separate Spring bean.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring Security offers three annotation styles for method-level authorization. Knowing which to use — and why the others exist — shows depth.

**`@PreAuthorize` — the standard choice**
- `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")` — simple role check
- `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('USER') and #id == authentication.name")` — the `#id` references the method parameter named `id`
- Evaluated before the method runs; access denied before any business logic executes

**`@PostAuthorize` — for ownership checks on return values**
- `@PostAuthorize("returnObject.ownerId == authentication.name")`
- The method runs first, then the expression is evaluated against the return value
- Use when you cannot determine authorization without knowing the result

**`@Secured` and `@RolesAllowed`**
- `@Secured({"ROLE_ADMIN", "ROLE_MANAGER"})` — Spring-specific; role string literals only
- `@RolesAllowed("ADMIN")` — JSR-250; Java standard; role strings only
- Both lack SpEL; use `@PreAuthorize` for anything beyond a simple role list

**Self-invocation trap**
- Method security is AOP-based; calling `this.method()` bypasses the proxy and skips security
- Always inject the bean and call through the proxy for method security to work
